questions.question: Explain the Decorator pattern in Java. How does it add behavior without subclassing?
questions.title: Decorator Pattern — Adding Behavior Without Subclassing
questions.direct_answer: The Decorator pattern wraps an object in another object that implements the same interface, adding behavior before or after delegating to the wrapped object. It avoids a class explosion from subclassing and enables composable behavior at runtime. Java I/O streams (BufferedInputStream wrapping FileInputStream) are the canonical example.

interviewer_intent.testing: Composition-over-inheritance understanding and ability to design extensible systems
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Decorator with Proxy — both wrap objects, but Decorator adds behavior while Proxy controls access
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference Java I/O streams as the most famous Decorator example, and Spring Security's filter chain as a real-world application

sections.title: The Class Explosion Problem That Inheritance Can't Solve
sections.content:
Imagine a `DataProcessor` with four optional behaviors: logging, encryption, compression, and validation. With inheritance, you'd need a subclass for every combination — `LoggingEncryptingDataProcessor`, `LoggingCompressingDataProcessor`, `EncryptingCompressingValidatingDataProcessor`. That's 2^4 = 16 subclasses, and adding a fifth behavior doubles it to 32.

The Decorator pattern eliminates this explosion through **composition**. Instead of extending a class, you wrap it. A decorator implements the **same interface** as the component it wraps and holds a reference to it. When a method is called, the decorator executes its added behavior (before or after) and delegates to the wrapped object. Multiple decorators stack like layers, each adding one responsibility.

The result is composable behavior at runtime. You build exactly the combination you need: `new LoggingDecorator(new EncryptionDecorator(new RawDataProcessor()))`. The outermost decorator processes first, delegates inward, and each layer is independent — removable, reorderable, and testable in isolation.

Java I/O streams are the most famous real-world Decorator. `new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(file)))` — three layers, each adding exactly one capability (buffering, character decoding, file reading), all sharing the `Reader` interface contract.

sections.title: The Mechanics: Same Interface, Wrapped Delegation, Composable Stacks
Java I/O Streams — The Most Famous Decorator You Use Every Day
sections.content:
Java's I/O library is built entirely on the Decorator pattern. `InputStream` is the component interface. `FileInputStream` is the concrete component that reads raw bytes from a file. `BufferedInputStream`, `GZIPInputStream`, `CipherInputStream` are decorators that wrap any `InputStream` and add one capability:

```java
// Three decorators stacked:
// CipherInputStream → GZIPInputStream → BufferedInputStream → FileInputStream
InputStream input = new CipherInputStream(
    new GZIPInputStream(
        new BufferedInputStream(
            new FileInputStream("/data/archive.gz.enc"))),
    cipher);
```

Each layer delegates to the next. `BufferedInputStream` adds buffering (reads in 8KB chunks instead of byte-by-byte). `GZIPInputStream` adds decompression. `CipherInputStream` adds decryption. Remove any layer and the rest still work — that's the power of the shared `InputStream` interface.

This design is why Java I/O feels composable but also verbose. You're constructing a pipeline of decorators explicitly, which gives you maximum flexibility at the cost of readability. Java's `Files.newBufferedReader()` convenience methods exist specifically to reduce this verbosity for common combinations.

Spring Security's filter chain follows the same principle. Each `Filter` wraps the next, adding one security check (authentication, authorization, CSRF, CORS) before delegating. The chain is a Decorator/Chain-of-Responsibility hybrid — each filter can either pass the request onward or reject it.

sections.title: Decorator vs Proxy: Same Wrapper, Different Intent
sections.content:
Both Decorator and Proxy wrap an object and implement the same interface. The structural mechanics are nearly identical — hold a reference, delegate method calls. The difference is **intent**.

**Decorator** adds behavior transparently. The caller doesn't know or care that logging, encryption, or compression was applied. The component's functionality is enhanced, not controlled. The client typically constructs the decorator chain explicitly.

**Proxy** controls access. A caching proxy intercepts calls and returns cached results without hitting the real object. A lazy-loading proxy defers expensive initialization until the first method call. A protection proxy checks permissions before delegating. Spring AOP proxies intercept `@Transactional` methods to manage transaction boundaries.

The practical test: if you're adding a new capability (logging, metrics, compression) → Decorator. If you're controlling how or whether the real object is accessed (caching, lazy loading, security checks, transaction management) → Proxy.

In Spring, `@Transactional` wraps your bean in a **proxy** that controls transaction lifecycle. The security filter chain is closer to a **decorator** that adds security checks to the request pipeline. Understanding this distinction helps you choose the right pattern and communicate your design decisions clearly.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Same interface contract** — decorator and component share the same interface, so callers never know they're talking to a decorator; this is what enables transparent stacking
- **Avoids class explosion** — 4 optional behaviors would require 16 inheritance subclasses; Decorator lets you compose any combination at runtime from 4 decorator classes
- **Java I/O is the canonical example** — `BufferedInputStream(GZIPInputStream(FileInputStream))` layers buffering and decompression over file reading, all through the `InputStream` interface
- **Spring Security filter chain** — a Decorator/Chain-of-Responsibility hybrid where each filter wraps the next, adding authentication, authorization, or CSRF checks before delegating
- **Decorator vs Proxy** — Decorator adds behavior transparently (logging, compression); Proxy controls access (caching, transactions, lazy loading); the structural mechanics are identical but the intent differs

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Decorator pattern solves a problem inheritance can't handle cleanly: **combining behaviors dynamically**. If a `DataProcessor` has four optional behaviors — logging, encryption, compression, validation — inheritance requires 16 subclasses for every combination. Decorator solves this with composition: each behavior is a wrapper class implementing the same interface that delegates to the wrapped object.

The mechanism is straightforward. A decorator holds a reference to another component with the same interface, adds its behavior before or after calling the wrapped method, and returns the result. Callers never know they're dealing with a decorator. You stack them at runtime in any order — the outermost decorator processes first and delegates inward.

Java I/O streams are the most famous example. `BufferedInputStream` wraps `FileInputStream`, and `GZIPInputStream` can wrap either. Each layer adds exactly one responsibility — buffering, compression, decryption — without modifying the others. This is why Java I/O feels composable, even if the explicit constructor chaining is verbose.

The interview distinction that matters is **Decorator vs Proxy**. Both wrap an object behind the same interface. Decorator adds behavior transparently — the caller doesn't know logging was added. Proxy controls access — caching, lazy loading, transaction management. Spring's `@Transactional` is a proxy pattern. The security filter chain is closer to a decorator chain. Same structural mechanics, different intent.

questions.question: How does the Proxy pattern work, and how does Spring AOP use it?
questions.title: Proxy Pattern — How Spring AOP Implements It
questions.direct_answer: The Proxy pattern provides a surrogate that controls access to another object. Spring AOP creates JDK dynamic proxies (for interface-based beans) or CGLIB proxies (for classes) at runtime. When a @Transactional or @Cacheable method is called, Spring intercepts the call through the proxy before/after reaching the real bean.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring's proxy mechanism and why self-invocation bypasses AOP
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling a @Transactional method from within the same class — self-invocation bypasses the proxy and the transaction is not started
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between JDK dynamic proxy and CGLIB, and when Spring uses each; mention AspectJ weaving as the non-proxy alternative

sections.title: Intercepting Method Calls Without Touching the Original Class
sections.content:
Every Spring developer uses the Proxy pattern daily — they just don't see it. When you annotate a method with `@Transactional`, Spring doesn't modify your class. Instead, it wraps your bean in a **proxy object** at application startup. The proxy implements the same interface (or extends the same class) as your bean. When any other bean calls a method on your service, the call hits the proxy first, which starts a transaction, delegates to your real method, and then commits or rolls back.

This is the Proxy pattern's core value: **adding cross-cutting concerns without modifying business logic**. Transactions, caching, security checks, async execution — all implemented through proxies that intercept method calls and execute infrastructure code around them.

The mechanism seems magical until something breaks. The most common Spring AOP bug — calling a `@Transactional` method from within the same class and wondering why the transaction doesn't start — is a direct consequence of how proxies work. Understanding the proxy mechanics isn't academic — it's the difference between debugging a production issue in 5 minutes vs 5 hours.

Spring uses two proxy strategies: **JDK dynamic proxies** for interface-based beans and **CGLIB** for class-based beans. Each has different constraints, and knowing which one is active for a given bean explains behaviors that otherwise seem random.

sections.title: JDK Dynamic Proxy: Interface-Based Interception at Runtime
CGLIB: Subclass-Based Proxying When There's No Interface
The Self-Invocation Trap — Why this.method() Bypasses Everything
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Self-invocation bypasses the proxy** — `this.transactionalMethod()` calls the real method directly; `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, `@Async` have no effect on internal calls within the same class
- **Self-invocation fixes** — extract the method into a separate bean (cleanest), inject the bean into itself (`@Autowired private OrderService self`), or switch to AspectJ compile-time weaving
- **CGLIB is Spring Boot's default** — since Spring Boot 2.0, `proxy-target-class=true` generates subclass proxies even when interfaces exist; CGLIB cannot proxy `final` classes or `final` methods
- **JDK dynamic proxy requires interfaces** — the proxy implements the interface, not the class; inject by interface type or you'll get `BeanNotOfRequiredType`
- **Proxy-powered annotations** — `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, `@PreAuthorize`, `@Async`, `@Retryable` all rely on proxies; understanding the mechanism explains why they silently fail in certain situations

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Proxy pattern places an intermediary between the caller and the real object. The proxy implements the same interface or extends the same class, so callers can't tell the difference. Inside the proxy, infrastructure logic runs before and after delegating to the real method — this is how **cross-cutting concerns** like transactions, caching, and security are applied without polluting business code.

Spring AOP is a production-scale implementation. When you annotate a method with `@Transactional`, Spring wraps the entire bean in a proxy at startup. Every call from outside goes through the proxy, which starts a transaction, delegates to your method, and commits or rolls back. `@Cacheable`, `@Async`, and `@PreAuthorize` work the same way.

Spring chooses between two proxy strategies. **JDK dynamic proxies** generate a class that implements the bean's interfaces — you must inject by interface type. **CGLIB** generates a subclass at runtime and is the default since Spring Boot 2.0. CGLIB can't proxy `final` classes or methods because it relies on subclassing.

The most important practical consequence is the **self-invocation trap**. If a `@Transactional` method calls another `@Transactional` method in the same class using `this.method()`, the call goes directly to the real object, bypassing the proxy. The transaction annotation on the inner call is silently ignored. The cleanest fix is moving the method to a separate bean so the call crosses bean boundaries and routes through the proxy.
